newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek election to decide Papandreou legacy.
newsitem.headline: Greek election to decide Papandreou legacy.

text.p: Greece voted on Sunday in a national election seen by pollsters as too close to call between the ruling socialists seeking a new four-year mandate and the challenging conservatives.

In their first electoral battle without their founding father Andreas Papandreou who died in June, the socialist PASOK party will find out if the Greek people want the torch bearers of socialism to remain in power.

Professorial Prime Minister Costas Simitis, 60, who succeeded Papandreou to the premiership in January, is pitted against conservative Miltiades Evert, 57, in an election which has lacked the drama Greeks demand from their politicians.

"PASOK is the party which has the resources and the positions to lead the country to the new age, to the world of the 21st century," Simitis told reporters after casting his vote in the working-class district of Kaminia in the port of Piraeus.
Papandreou's controversial blonde widow, Dimitra Liani, provided the colour on an otherwise lacklustre voting day.

Dressed in mourning black she turned up at her hometown of Elefsina, near Athens, to vote. She told reporters: "I vote on behalf of Andreas Papandreou, the great absent protagonist of these elections."
Simitis, a bland technocrat, called the early election confident he was far ahead in polls but soon saw the conservative's snapping at his heels.
His passionless, media-oriented campaign failed to inspire the voters or get them out on the street, prompting the press to dub the contest the "couch elections".
The outspoken Evert, a former Athens mayor, was optimistic after he voted in a remote village near the Evros River, a natural border between Greece and Turkey.
"Words from politicians are redundant. Today the Greek people speak and I believe tomorrow will be a new, great day for Greece," Evert said.

Evert, who has made Athens acrimonious relationship with Ankara the battlecry of his campaign and who did not shy away from making populist pledges to woo voters, has steadily risen in public opinion polls.

Poll analysts say this is the hardest Greek election to call, with an unprecedented number of undecided voters and a clear turn to smaller parties. The socialists are leading slightly and within the margin of error.

A far cry from Papandreou's fiery balcony oratories against Western imperialism, Simitis's views differ little from his conservative adversary's, especially on what is needed to turn the ailing economy around.
Without significant differences, the campaign quickly became a personality contest, but with both contenders lacking charisma, the public has remained largely indifferent to this election.
Pollsters said an unusually high 20 percent of those asked one week before elections said they were undecided about how they would cast their ballot.
"It is too close to call. Everything about this election is new -- the leaders, the number of undecided voters, the general apathy," poll analyst Ilias Nikolakopoulos said on television.
Simitis, a strongly pro-European technocrat, is nothing like his mentor, the flamboyant Papandreou, who died in June after a long illness.
The maverick socialist leader's pledges of free-spending socialism to aid the underprivileged secured him three landslide victories in 1981, 1985 and 1993.
About 8.5 million Greeks are required to cast a mandatory vote at polling stations around the country, which opened at sunrise at 0413 GMT and will close at sunset at 1620 GMT.
The first exit poll results will be made public after official voting ends.
